title: Trees: Invert a Binary Tree
oneLiner: Mirror a binary tree by swapping every node's left and right children. The smallest useful example of "do something at each node, then recurse".
keyTakeaway: Inverting a tree is one rule applied everywhere: swap this node's two children, then invert both subtrees (or invert them first and swap after; either order works). Every node is visited once, O(n), and the recursion is as deep as the tree, O(h). A queue gives the same result iteratively.
explanation:
Invert a binary tree, meaning mirror it left to right, and return its root. [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9] becomes [4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]: the whole left side moves to the right and every level reads backwards.

Think about what the mirror of a tree is. The root stays put. Its new left subtree is the mirror of its old right subtree, and its new right subtree is the mirror of its old left subtree. That definition is already the code: if the node is null, return null; otherwise invert both children and assign them swapped, root.Left = Invert(old right) and root.Right = Invert(old left).

Watch the classic slip: writing root.Left = Invert(root.Right) and then root.Right = Invert(root.Left) reads root.Left after you already overwrote it. Save one side in a variable first, or use a tuple swap that evaluates both sides before assigning.

Every node is visited once, so O(n) time. The recursion goes as deep as the tree is tall: O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a chain. To avoid deep recursion, put the root in a queue (or stack), and for each node you take out, swap its children and add the non-null ones. Any visiting order works because each node's swap is independent of the others.

The visualization inverts [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9] top down, one swap per step.

pythonHarnessPreamble:
null = None

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def build_level_order_tree(values):
    # Builds a tree from a level-order list; null (None) marks a missing child.
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(values):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if values[i] is not None:
            node.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:
            node.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root

def tree_to_list(root):
    # The tree as a level-order list with None for missing children, trailing Nones trimmed.
    result = []
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if node is None:
            result.append(None)
            continue
        result.append(node.val)
        queue.append(node.left)
        queue.append(node.right)
    while result and result[-1] is None:
        result.pop()
    return result
recognitionSignals: "Mirror", "flip" or "invert" a tree, or check whether two trees are mirrors (Symmetric Tree).
A change that applies the same way at every node independently: any traversal order will do.
gotchas: Overwriting root.Left before reading it for the right side loses a subtree.
Forgetting the null base case crashes on leaves' children.
Swapping values instead of child pointers only works for complete trees and is not what is asked.
confusableWith: Symmetric Tree compares a tree with its own mirror without building it, walking two pointers in opposite directions.
Diameter of a Binary Tree also recurses on both children, but combines their results; here there is nothing to combine.

complexity.note: Each node is visited and swapped once. The recursion stack is as deep as the tree is tall, h: O(log n) balanced, O(n) for a chain. (A BFS version uses a queue that can hold a whole level, O(n).)
